commenti.body:
> as if we have experienced eternity   
What a turn of phrase. This is a great interview, so much less aggro than the earlier ones posted here--or it might just be that he clearly lives these films. I want to rewatch all of them now, even though it's only been a couple years.

Thanks for listing this. I wish more director’s would give breakdowns on films they admire as they often have such fascinating perspective’s on them that no one else seems to see. Scorsese does this a lot I know, but I practically think of him as a film critic or historian as well as a filmmaker. It’s like Spielberg’s brief comments on Dune 2 and his point on how the entire film is permeated with a thirst and yearning for water—both physically and spiritually. Or like Guillermo Del Toro’s analysis of “Memories of Murder” [(seen here)](https://youtu.be/uOI8filpgZI?si=lJgRth5YzayKNQFK), who gave some of the best insights into that film out there.

Interesting interview. This made me choke:


>The first time I saw Blade Runner, I went to the cinema, and I felt there was no need for a voiceover at all. It was so wordy. But in the later "Director's Cut," the voiceover was removed, and the film suddenly became harmonious. It's actually best to let the audience gradually understand the protagonist during the viewing process. American films don't always need voiceovers.


GITS2 is one of the wordiest, talkiest movies around, completely let down by how verbose it is. Director, heal thyself!

> I absolutely agree about the comments on budget

> So, what happens when a director has unlimited money to support what they truly want to do? The answer is – they become Francis Ford Coppola

Very timely.

If you watch the documentary Hearts of Darkness there’s some pretty extensive interviews with George Lucas about how he offered a bunch of advice to Francis Ford Coppola on directing Apocalypse Now…advice George Lucas followed none of himself when directing Episode I, II and III. Pretty funny how directors do that.

Really interesting interview, thanks for posting. You can tell how passionate Oshii is about filmmaking, how intensely he studies and contemplates the films he enjoys. That obsession and desires to break down and understand how scenes and effects in blade runner were accomplished brought him much insight. I wonder what he thinks about Tarkovsky's films. His comments about how film can manipulate our sense of time reminds me of Tarkovsky and Deleuze in their conception of film as a primarily time based medium.

For sure--though it is funny that it refers here to an exhibit of flagrant excess now decades old and enshrined as one of the greats. Not that Oshii cares, this wouldn't be an Oshii review if he didn't drop some incredibly divisive opinion as if it was common knowledge.   

I still want to see Megalopolis, fwiw, though I'm not at all sure I'll make it through the whole thing. I tapped out of Babylon about halfway through because of its overripe nonsense and it sounds like Megalopolis may be similarly decadent.

I recommend looking out for editions of [Projections](https://www.goodreads.com/series/285874-projections), a book series published by Faber and edited by John Boorman (!). Each issue features a wide variety of articles written by directors and other industry figures, and often includes what you’re looking for here - directors writing about other directors and their movies. Best of all, in the UK at least, they’re dirt cheap on eBay - I’ve been picking them up in bundle offers and paying around £3 per book. Every one so far has been worth a lot more than that.

There’s also a best of collection ([Director’s Cut](https://www.faber.co.uk/product/9780571233151-directors-cut/)), which I expect is a solid alternative to buying them all.

You're right. In other interviews, he's made some pretty controversial statements, including some inappropriate jokes (for example, he likened the pre-transition Wachowskis to a gay married couple). While those comments don't represent the entirety of his views, I think they'd overshadow everything else and I'd get absolutely buried in downvotes.
I'm not sure I understood what Oshii means when he says Apocalypse Now and Space Odyssey are failures. Does he literally mean that?

Regarding "Apocalypse Now", Oshii didn't say much. However, there's an entire interview about "2001: A Space Odyssey", which is the first piece in this book. He chose it as the representative work of 1968, considering it the first film to truly express the concept of "universe" through cinematic language, successfully visualizing "cosmic time".

Oshii greatly appreciated this work (along with "A Clockwork Orange") in his youth. However, he's not particularly fond of Kubrick's later works. In his own words: "From a director's perspective, he became increasingly boring once he started playing the role of a perfectionist."

Of course, this doesn't explain why Oshii said "2001: A Space Odyssey" was a failure in some sense, as he didn't specify what he meant by "in some sense". I can't answer on his behalf, but I can say that overall, he does like "2001: A Space Odyssey".
